Ukraine’s expected arrival of Gripen C fighters armed with Meteor missiles could pose a serious new threat to Russian aviation, particularly aircraft responsible for launching glide bombs. The implications could extend well beyond air-to-air combat. tweet

The United States has postponed the announcement of the results of its review of the US military presence in Europe, initially scheduled for December, until next year , the Brussels-based Rapporteur portal reported, citing diplomatic sources. The review process, initiated by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth in June, was scheduled to last six months, with its findings due to be presented in December. Its goal is to reduce the US military presence in Europe and cut the amount of resources Washington could provide to its NATO allies in the event of a crisis.

🇺🇸 US plans training for Syrian military with 15 nations Washington is considering launching an international programme to train Syrian servicemen in demining and neutralising unexploded ordnance. Training could begin in March 2027 in Syria and Jordan. Around 15 states, including the UK, France, Germany, Australia, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, may join the initiative. American involvement is expected to be limited. The plan was discussed on November 12 by Syrian Defence Minister Murhaf Abu Qasra and US Admiral Liam Hulin. It could expand Washington-Damascus cooperation. Implementation faces hurdles due to US legal requirements for human rights vetting of Syrian units and internal disagreements within Damascus's military leadership. Estimated funding is around $200 million. @Slavyangrad

Iran's 358 loitering surface-to-air missile system was displayed atop a camouflage-covered mound at the "Miracle of Science and Faith" exhibition in Mashhad, Iran, which opened on November 25, 2026. The 358 missile, placed on a display stand on the left side of the exhibit, is a subsonic, turbojet-powered loitering munition designed to patrol an area and engage low- to medium-altitude aerial targets, including drones and helicopters. It relies on passive optical and infrared sensors rather than active radar for target acquisition and engagement. The system has been used to shoot down several U.S. and Israeli unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). The display also includes the system's control and communications equipment: a ruggedized laptop/console unit on the central table and a tripod-mounted dish antenna on the right, identified in the accompanying caption as the uplink and downlink equipment.
